questions.q:
Two imaginary sites are excavated and both are accepted as Harappan cities. City A lies on a river plain and is built of brick. City B lies where stone is locally plentiful and is built mostly of stone, with its highest area fortified.
(a) Which of the two fits the chapter's usual pattern for Harappan cities, and what reason does the chapter give for that pattern?
(b) A visitor says City B contradicts the chapter's statement about materials. Does it? Name the real Harappan city that shows the same thing.
(c) The chapter describes the gate of that real city's highest area. What would you expect to find beside the gate of City B's highest area?
(d) The visitor concludes, 'So the chapter was wrong to call brick the usual material.' Judge this.
questions.a: (a) City A: most Harappan cities were built of bricks, as they lay on alluvial plains where clay is abundant. (b) No. Dholavira, unlike most others, made extensive use of stone because it was locally available; the chapter says 'most', so an exception does not contradict it. (c) A large sentinel room, where guards would have screened people moving in or out, and smooth blocks of stone. (d) Not justified: the chapter itself says most cities used brick and that Dholavira was unlike most others, so one stone city is a noted exception, not a refutation.
s: Part (a): City A, brick because clay is abundant on alluvial plains
Part (b): no; Dholavira used local stone, and the chapter says 'most'
Part (c): a sentinel room where guards would have screened people
Part (d): an exception the chapter itself notes does not make 'usual' wrong

questions.q: A town planner wants to borrow ideas from Mohenjo-daro for a new neighbourhood. (a) Name two features of Mohenjo-daro's streets or its large house that she could borrow, with the chapter's detail for each. (b) The chapter calls Harappan architecture the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction. What does this tell her about the thing the Harappan builders planned? (c) She decides to build everything in brick 'because Mohenjo-daro did'. Using Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, say what the chapter lets her conclude about choosing a material.
questions.a: (a) Wide streets and narrow lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions; the large house, where the servants probably lived downstairs and the owners upstairs, less exposed to the dust and noise of the streets. (b) That they planned whole cities, with carefully laid-out plans and standardised urban concepts, not single buildings. (c) Mohenjo-daro used brick because it lay on alluvial plains where clay is abundant, while Dholavira used much stone because it was locally available; so the material should follow what the place supplies, and brick is not the rule everywhere.
s: Part (a): two features with the chapter's detail
Part (b): whole cities, laid out with standardised urban concepts
Part (c): material follows local availability; Dholavira used stone

questions.q:
A museum must choose one of two captions for a photograph of the entrance to the highest and most fortified area of Dholavira.
Caption X: 'The eastern entrance of the Castle: smooth blocks of stone, and on the left a large sentinel room where guards would have screened people moving in or out. Two highly polished segments of a stone pillar remain visible in the centre.'
Caption Y: 'The eastern entrance of the Castle: guards checked every visitor in the sentinel room, and the pillar in the centre carried the city's flag.'
(a) Which caption does the chapter support?
(b) Name the detail in the other caption that the chapter does not state at all.
(c) Why does Caption X say 'would have screened' instead of 'screened'?
(d) What name does the chapter give to this highest area, and for what quality is Dholavira 'noted'?
questions.a: (a) Caption X. (b) That the pillar carried the city's flag; the chapter says only that two highly polished segments of a stone pillar remain visible in the centre. (c) The guards' role is the chapter's reading of the sentinel room, not a recorded fact, so it is worded as likely. (d) The Castle; Dholavira is noted for its precise urban planning.
s: Part (a): Caption X
Part (b): the flag; only polished pillar segments are stated
Part (c): the screening is an inference, so 'would have'
Part (d): Castle; precise urban planning

questions.q: The chapter calls the Castle the highest and most fortified area of Dholavira. (a) Which detail of its eastern entrance suggests that people moving in or out were checked? (b) A student concludes that ordinary families lived inside the Castle. Does the chapter give any support for this?
questions.a: (a) The large sentinel room on the left, where guards would have screened people moving in or out. (b) No. The chapter says nothing about who lived in the Castle; the details it gives (fortification and the guard room) point to defence and control of movement.
s: Part (a): the large sentinel room where guards would have screened people
Part (b): the chapter gives no support; it says nothing about who lived there

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Harappan architecture is described as the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction in the Indian subcontinent.
Reason (R): Most Harappan cities were built of bricks because they lay on alluvial plains where clay is abundant.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter promises a complete survey of the evolution, diversity and technicalities of Indian architecture.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that exploring all of it cannot be done in a brief chapter, so it offers a journey through a few representative structures grouped in a few categories.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a brief chapter cannot cover everything, so only a few representative structures in a few categories are visited

questions.q: Ritu, an architecture student, tells her friend: 'Architecture is only about making a building look beautiful; the technical side belongs to somebody else.' Which reply matches how the chapter defines architecture?
questions.a: It joins functional and aesthetic aspects, and is a technical field as well as an art
o: It joins functional and aesthetic aspects, and is a technical field as well as an art
It is the art of ornament, with the techniques of construction treated as a separate subject taught elsewhere
It is the technique of building safe structures, and beauty is added only when funds permit
It is the study of past monuments, grouped by period

questions.q: Write a description of three or four lines for an imaginary Harappan-style town that has all of these: carefully laid-out streets, a fortified high area, and a building material suited to the site. Then label which part of the chapter's account each line follows.
questions.a: Sample: 'The town's wide streets and narrow lanes run roughly in the cardinal directions. At the top stands a fortified Castle, with a sentinel room at its gate. As the hills nearby give plenty of stone, the walls are of stone, not brick.' Labels: laid-out plan (like Mohenjo-daro's cardinal orientation); fortified high area (like Dholavira's Castle with its sentinel room); material suited to the site (like Dholavira's locally available stone).
s: A laid-out street plan, labelled
A fortified high area with a gate arrangement, labelled
A material tied to what the place supplies, labelled

questions.q: A student's outline map puts Mohenjo-daro in the Rann of Kachchh and Dholavira in Sindh. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: Mohenjo-daro is in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, and Dholavira is in the Rann of Kachchh
o: Mohenjo-daro is in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, and Dholavira is in the Rann of Kachchh
Both cities lie in the Rann of Kachchh, which was one large Harappan region of cities
Both cities lie in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, and Dholavira is its northern city
Mohenjo-daro is in Sindh and Dholavira is in a part of Pakistan beside the Rann of Kachchh

questions.q: Explain how three parts of the chapter's description of Harappan cities show that their builders thought about the whole city, not about single buildings.
questions.a: (1) The chapter calls Harappan architecture carefully laid-out cities with standardised urban concepts, so the plan came before the buildings. (2) At Mohenjo-daro, wide streets and narrow lanes were roughly oriented to the cardinal directions across an extensive city. (3) Dholavira is noted for precise urban planning, with differently fortified areas, streets and reservoirs shown on its plan.
s: Laid-out cities and standardised concepts
Mohenjo-daro's oriented streets and lanes across an extensive city
Dholavira's precise plan with fortified areas, streets and reservoirs

questions.q: A student reads the chapter's timeline for the date given to Dholavira and, for the Sanchi Stupa, takes the earliest possible date in the 3rd century BCE, 300 BCE. The gap between the two is ___ years.

(a) Name the two illustrations that guide the chapter's journey and say what each shows. (b) A student wants to know which of two monuments in the chapter is the older. Which of the two guides should she use, and why?
questions.a: (a) The map (Fig. 3.3) shows the geographical locations of the structures to be visited; the timeline (Fig. 3.2) places them in the river of time. (b) The timeline, because it shows where each structure falls in time, while the map shows only where it stands.
s: Part (a): the map shows locations; the timeline places the structures in time
Part (b): the timeline, since the question is about age, not place

questions.q: Arjun says: 'Everything the chapter says about Harappan architecture is about brick; there is no stone at all, and every Harappan city had the same layout.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. 'Everything is about brick' and 'no stone at all' are both wrong: the chapter says most Harappan cities were built of bricks but that Dholavira, unlike most others, made extensive use of locally available stone. 'The same layout' is also unsupported: the chapter describes Mohenjo-daro's lanes oriented to the cardinal directions and Dholavira's fortified Castle with different areas, streets and reservoirs, and never says the plans were identical.
s: 'Everything about brick' wrong: the chapter says most, not all, cities used brick
'No stone at all' wrong: Dholavira used much local stone; 'same layout' not supported
Verdict: No

questions.q:
Match each Harappan observation in Column A with what the chapter links it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Almost every home has a bathing area, and used water leaves the city by drains.  2. Streets and lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions.  3. Smooth stone blocks and a large room where guards screened visitors.  4. Walls of brick throughout the city.
Column B: a. A fortified entrance to the highest area of a city  b. Alluvial plains where clay is abundant  c. A carefully laid-out city plan  d. An emphasis on drainage and water management

The chapter says Mohenjo-daro's streets and lanes were 'roughly oriented to the cardinal directions'. A student writes: 'So the builders used exact compass instruments, and every lane ran exactly north-south or east-west.' (a) What does the chapter actually say about the orientation? (b) Which two parts of the student's sentence go beyond it?
questions.a: (a) That the wide streets and narrow lanes were roughly oriented to the cardinal directions. (b) The use of exact compass instruments, which the chapter does not mention, and 'exactly', since the chapter says only 'roughly'.
s: Part (a): roughly oriented to the cardinal directions
Part (b): compass instruments and 'exactly' go beyond the chapter

questions.q: The chapter says that in the large Mohenjo-daro house the servants lived downstairs while the owners 'probably' lived upstairs. (a) What reason does it give for the owners' being upstairs? (b) A student adds: 'So the owner must have been a merchant, since only merchants kept servants.' Does the chapter allow this? (c) Why is 'probably' the right word?
questions.a: (a) Upstairs they would be less exposed to the dust and noise from the streets around. (b) No. The chapter says nothing about the owner's occupation or about who kept servants. (c) The plan only hints at how the rooms were used; nobody recorded it, so the chapter gives it as an inference.
s: Part (a): less exposed to dust and noise from the streets
Part (b): no; nothing about the owner's occupation
Part (c): the plan only hints, so it is an inference

questions.q: A site report on a large house in an ancient brick city notes two floors joined by a stair. The lower floor has small rooms opening on a noisy lane. Which inference would the chapter support in the case of the large house in Mohenjo-daro?
questions.a: Servants probably downstairs, owners upstairs, away from street dust and noise
o: Servants probably downstairs, owners upstairs, away from street dust and noise
The owners lived downstairs to keep near the lane, and the servants slept in the upper rooms of the house
Both floors were rented out to traders, since a lane-facing room was valued as a shop
The lower floor was a bathing hall for the whole street, and the upper floor a granary

questions.q: (a) Give the chapter's meaning of 'architecture'. (b) Using (a), say in one sentence why a richly carved gateway that cracks and falls during its first season would count as a failure of architecture even though it looked beautiful.
questions.a: (a) Architecture is the art and techniques of design and construction, which combine functional and aesthetic aspects. (b) The gateway met only the aesthetic aspect; architecture must combine it with the functional, so a structure that does not do its job fails the definition however fine it looks.
s: Part (a): art and techniques of design and construction combining functional and aesthetic aspects
Part (b): beauty alone is not enough; the functional aspect is also required

questions.q: Neha says: 'Dholavira's gateway of smooth stone blocks proves it was not a Harappan city, because Harappan cities were built of brick.' What does the chapter allow you to answer?
questions.a: It is a Harappan city that, unlike most, used much stone since stone was locally available
o: It is a Harappan city that, unlike most, used much stone since stone was locally available
It is a Harappan city whose stone came from distant quarries since local clay was poor in quality
It is a later city built on the Harappan site after brick had gone out of fashion in the region
It is a Harappan city whose stone gateway was added after the planned city had been built

questions.q:
Three students make statements about Harappan cities. Judge each as right, wrong or partly right, giving the chapter's evidence.
S1: 'Mohenjo-daro lies in the Rann of Kachchh.'
S2: 'Dholavira is noted for its precise urban planning.'
S3: 'The plan of the large Mohenjo-daro house proves the servants lived downstairs and the owners upstairs.'
(d) Rewrite S1 and S3 so that each is correct.
questions.a: S1: wrong; Mohenjo-daro is in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, and the Rann of Kachchh is where Dholavira lies. S2: right; the chapter calls Dholavira noted for its precise urban planning. S3: partly right; the plan hints at the arrangement and the owners 'probably' lived upstairs, but it is an inference, not proof. (d) S1: 'Mohenjo-daro lies in present-day Sindh, Pakistan.' S3: 'The plan of the large Mohenjo-daro house hints that the servants lived downstairs and the owners probably upstairs.'
s: S1 judged wrong with the correct location
S2 judged right with the chapter's evidence
S3 judged partly right: a hint, not proof
Part (d): S1 rewritten correctly
Part (d): S3 rewritten with 'hints' or 'probably'

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harappan cities.
1. Mohenjo-daro had wide streets and narrow lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions.
2. Used water from Mohenjo-daro's bathing areas was collected in pits inside each home.
3. Dholavira, in the Rann of Kachchh, is noted for its precise urban planning.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The chapter says the stone railings of the Bharhut stupa bore numerous inscriptions recording donors' names, and that the main stupa at Sanchi was 'originally commissioned or patronised by' Ashoka. (a) What do the Bharhut inscriptions tell us about how such a stupa came to be built? (b) What does the Sanchi sentence add, and why does it not rule out donors there?
questions.a: (a) That donors contributed to it, since their names were recorded on the railings. (b) It adds that Sanchi's main stupa had a royal commissioner or patron, Ashoka; the chapter does not say he alone paid, so donors are not ruled out.
s: Part (a): donors contributed, as their names are recorded
Part (b): Sanchi had a royal patron, but the chapter does not exclude donors

questions.q:
An imaginary hillside complex, Z, was begun in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage. Over the following centuries the patrons changed, and so did the needs of the monks who used it.
(a) Predict, using the chapter's general statement on rock-cut complexes, what will be true of Z after several centuries.
(b) A scholar finds that Z's caves differ in age, some used for living and some for assembly. Does this fit the chapter?
(c) Another scholar says all of Z's caves must be of one date because one king began it. Judge this.
(d) Name the Odisha complex the chapter describes as begun in the 2nd century BCE, and say what most of its caves served as.
questions.a: (a) Such complexes often evolved over centuries, reflecting changing religious needs and patronage, so Z will have been added to and changed. (b) Yes: caves for worship, residence or assembly are the three uses the chapter lists, and a complex that evolved will hold caves of different ages. (c) Not supported: the chapter says carving began under royal patronage but that such complexes often evolved over centuries, so a start by one king does not fix every cave's date. (d) The Udayagiri-Khandagiri complex near Bhubaneswar; most of its caves served as dwellings for Jain monks.
s: Part (a): evolved over centuries with changing needs and patronage
Part (b): yes; caves of worship, residence or assembly of different ages fit
Part (c): the start under one king does not fix all dates; complexes evolve
Part (d): Udayagiri-Khandagiri; dwellings for Jain monks

questions.q:
Match each feature in Column A with the monument the chapter links it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Massive toranas and a railing (vedika) inside which worshippers walked.  2. Stone railings with inscriptions recording donors' names.  3. Caves begun in the 2nd century BCE, mostly dwellings.  4. An arched roof imitating timber beams.
Column B: a. Bharhut stupa  b. Ellora cave no. 10  c. Udayagiri-Khandagiri  d. Main stupa at Sanchi
Differentiate between a structural stupa and a rock-cut cave complex on (a) how each is made and (b) what each is used for, as the chapter describes them.
questions.a: (a) A stupa is a dome-shaped structure raised from brick or stone; a cave complex is made by carving directly into the rock. (b) A stupa houses relics of the Buddha or of revered monks (the larger ones becoming ritual centres); caves serve as places for worship, residence or assembly.
s: Part (a): built up in brick or stone vs carved into rock
Part (b): relics and ritual centre vs worship, residence or assembly

questions.q: The Buddha statue leaning against the stupa in Ellora's cave no. 10 is a seated human figure in a teaching pose. Show that this statue cannot be used as an example of how the Buddha was shown 'at this early stage' of stupa architecture.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says that at the early stage the Buddha was represented symbolically, through footprints, the wheel of dharma or the stupa itself. (2) The statue in cave no. 10 is a massive human figure of the seated Buddha in a teaching pose. (3) A human figure is exactly what the early stage did without, so the statue is not an example of the early symbolic representation.
s: Early stage: symbols such as footprints, wheel, stupa
Cave no. 10's statue is a human figure
So it cannot illustrate the early symbolic stage

questions.q: The chapter says the carving at Udayagiri-Khandagiri 'began' in the 2nd century BCE. (a) What does the word 'began' leave open? (b) A student says the whole complex was carved in a single year. Does the chapter allow this?
questions.a: (a) It gives only the starting date and leaves open when later caves were cut. (b) No. The chapter says such complexes often evolved over centuries, so a single year is not supported.
s: Part (a): it gives only the start, not the date of the last cave
Part (b): no, since complexes often evolved over centuries

questions.q: The chapter says carving Ellora's monolithic Kailasha Temple meant chipping away 'many thousands of tonnes of rock'. (a) What does 'monolithic' tell you about how the temple was made? (b) What else does the chapter say Ellora contains besides the Kailasha Temple? (c) What two qualities does the chapter give for rock-cut construction, and for whom is it said to have developed?
questions.a: (a) A monolithic temple is one block: the builders carved it out of the rock, leaving the temple standing, rather than assembling it from separate pieces. (b) Many Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. (c) It developed as an efficient and durable mode of construction for religious communities.
s: Part (a): carved out of the rock as one piece
Part (b): many Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves
Part (c): efficient and durable, for religious communities

questions.q: A visitor notes that most of the small caves at Udayagiri-Khandagiri look like living quarters. The chapter says most of them served as dwellings for ___ monks.
questions.a: Jain

questions.q: A model-maker is building a model of Ellora's cave no. 10 and must decide what goes where. (a) Which two figures must she place together in the hall, and what shape must she give the roof? (b) The roof shape reminds a visitor of buildings in towns. Which buildings does the chapter mean? (c) Where must she leave a corridor, and what would monks do in it? (d) A friend says the corridor is a waste of effort. Using the name of the custom, say why the chapter would disagree.
questions.a: (a) A stupa and a massive statue of the seated Buddha in a teaching pose, leaning against it; the roof is arched. (b) Some of the urban buildings that had beams of timber, which the arched roof imitates. (c) In the aisle, the corridor outside the row of pillars, where monks would circumambulate the stupa. (d) The walking round is pradakshina, 'going around in a clockwise direction', a custom the chapter says will persist in later classical temples, so the corridor is part of how the cave was used.
s: Part (a): stupa and seated Buddha statue, with an arched roof
Part (b): urban buildings with timber beams
Part (c): the aisle outside the pillars, where monks circumambulate the stupa
Part (d): pradakshina, clockwise going around
Part (d): it persists in later classical temples, so the corridor has a purpose

questions.q: A guide has to use Sanchi and Bharhut to show three things to visitors. For each, say which stupa she should use and the chapter's evidence: (a) gateways that show many scenes of urban and village life; (b) records of who gave support; (c) a carving that shows worship of the stupa. (d) Name one thing both share. (e) Using your answers, say why the chapter calls the larger stupas 'complex ritual centres'.
questions.a: (a) Sanchi: its massive toranas are ornamental gateways depicting many scenes of urban as well as village life. (b) Bharhut: its richly carved stone railings bore numerous inscriptions recording donors' names. (c) Bharhut: a panel depicts people worshipping the stupa there. (d) Both stupas were enclosed by railings (the vedika at Sanchi). (e) Railings, gateways and elaborate panels, with worship, walking around and donations, made them more than a dome, so they were complex ritual centres.
s: Part (a): Sanchi's toranas with scenes of urban and village life
Part (b): Bharhut's donor inscriptions
Part (c): Bharhut's panel showing worship
Part (d): railings enclose both stupas
Part (e): railings, gateways and panels made them ritual centres, not just domes

questions.q: At a Jain site a visitor finds a dome-shaped structure and says: 'Stupas are only Buddhist, so this cannot be one.' Which reply matches the chapter?
questions.a: Stupas are common in Jainism too, in diverse dimensions and shapes
o: Stupas are common in Jainism too, in diverse dimensions and shapes
Stupas belong to Buddhism alone, so the Jain dome must be a cave dwelling for monks cut into the hillside
Stupas were first built by Jains, and Buddhists took over the dome form at Sanchi and Bharhut only later
Stupas are found in Jainism only in caves, and never as dome-shaped structures built of brick or stone

questions.q: Rahul says: 'Stupas were built of brick or stone, and only Buddhists ever built them.' Test each half against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the chapter says thousands of stupas were constructed with bricks or stone. The second half is wrong: the chapter says stupas are common in Jainism too.
s: First half right: brick or stone
Second half wrong: stupas are common in Jainism too
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: A tour guide tells a group: 'The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were begun in the 2nd century CE as assembly halls for Buddhist monks.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: Carving began in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage, and most caves were dwellings for Jain monks
o: Carving began in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage, and most caves were dwellings for Jain monks
Carving began in the 2nd century BCE, and most caves were assembly halls for Jain monks
Carving began in the 2nd century CE under royal patronage, and most caves were temples to Shiva
Carving began in the 4th century BCE, and most caves were dwellings for monks of any faith

questions.q: Write a four-line guide for a pilgrim at Sanchi, telling her in order what she meets and does, so that your lines use the words torana, vedika and circumambulate correctly. Then say in one line what the toranas show.
questions.a: Sample: 'Come to the main stupa in Madhya Pradesh. First pass under one of the massive toranas, the ornamental gateways. Inside, you stand within the railing, the vedika. Now circumambulate: walk around the stupa.' The toranas show many scenes of urban as well as village life.
s: A guide that uses torana as the entrance gateway and vedika as the railing enclosure
Circumambulate used correctly as walking around the stupa, in a sensible order
Toranas show many scenes of urban and village life

questions.q:
Read the statements about stupas.
1. At the early stage the Buddha was usually shown in human form on stupa panels.
2. The stupa at Bharhut was enclosed by richly carved stone railings and bore inscriptions recording donors' names.
3. Stupas are found in Jainism too.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False? 'The main stupa at Sanchi represents the earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture in India, and a worshipper entered it through a massive torana.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the main stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh represents the earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture in India; a worshipper entered through one of its massive toranas, ornamental gateways showing many scenes of urban and village life.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture; entry through massive toranas with scenes of urban and village life

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The roof of the Ellora cave no. 10 is flat.
Reason (R): The arched roof of the cave imitates beams of timber that existed in some of the urban buildings.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: (a) The arched roof of Ellora's cave no. 10 imitates something. What does it imitate? (b) Using (a), say what this tells you about the buildings the carvers had in front of them.
questions.a: (a) It imitates beams of timber. (b) Some urban buildings of the time had timber beams, so the carvers copied the look of those buildings in stone; the cave's design was borrowed from buildings seen in towns.
s: Part (a): beams of timber
Part (b): some urban buildings had such beams, so the carvers copied their form

questions.q:
Two students wrote notes on the main stupa at Sanchi.
Note P: 'It represents the earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture in India.'
Note Q: 'It is the first building ever made of stone in India.'
(a) Which note does the chapter support?
(b) Name the earlier city in this chapter that already used much stone, which shows that Note Q cannot stand.
(c) A third note says the stupa was built by Ashoka personally. What exact wording does the chapter use, and how does it differ?
(d) Rewrite Note Q so that it is acceptable.
questions.a: (a) Note P. (b) Dholavira, which made extensive use of stone, as it was locally available. (c) The chapter says the stupa was 'originally commissioned or patronised by' Ashoka, which does not say he built it himself and leaves open whether he commissioned it or only patronised it. (d) For example: 'It represents the earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture in India.'
s: Part (a): Note P
Part (b): Dholavira used much stone
Part (c): 'commissioned or patronised', not 'built personally'
Part (d): a rewrite that keeps 'earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture'

questions.q: In a classical temple, a pilgrim walks clockwise around the shrine along a corridor. Which practice from earlier architecture in this concept does the chapter say this continues?
questions.a: Pradakshina, as when monks of Ellora's cave no. 10 walked around the stupa
o: Pradakshina, as when monks of Ellora's cave no. 10 walked around the stupa
Pradakshina, as when donors' names were carved on the railings of a stupa at Bharhut and Sanchi
The use of a stambha as a flag post, as at stupa gateways
The carving of arched roofs, as in the aisle of an early brick stupa

questions.q: A guide at Ellora tells visitors that the colossal Kailasha Temple was built by stacking large stone blocks, one over another. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: It was carved out of the rock itself as a monolithic temple
o: It was carved out of the rock itself as a monolithic temple
It was built of brick and plastered over, then painted to look like the hill's rock
It was assembled from carved blocks that were hauled from distant hills by many workers

questions.q:
