(b) Any two of: Egypt's pyramids and temples, Athens' Parthenon, medieval Europe's gothic cathedrals. (c) The 10th century; any two of multiple shrines, amenities and enclosures (prakaras). (d) For example, a vimana over 60 metres high, or a massive Nandi carved from a single stone. So faith and labour alone do not describe it: skill and mathematics were needed too.
s: Part (a): four kinds of skill or knowledge from the chapter
Part (b): two comparisons from Egypt, Athens or medieval Europe
Part (c): the 10th century and two things the complexes began to include
Part (d): a scale detail of the Brihadishvara Temple
A conclusion answering Raju

questions.q:
A scholar notes that Sharada Peetha is now in ruins, yet the chapter calls it an important part of India's heritage.
(a) What does the chapter say the temple was renowned for, and for which script was it a key site?
(b) What name did its legacy earn for Kashmir?
(c) How can a ruin still be called important heritage? Answer from the chapter.
(d) A student says it flourished for under 300 years. The chapter says it flourished between the 6th and 12th centuries CE. Judge the student, using the narrowest reading (end of the 6th century to the start of the 12th).
questions.a: (a) A renowned centre of learning that attracted scholars from different parts of India and the world; a key site in the development of the Sharada script. (b) Sharada Desh, the land of Sharada. (c) The chapter says that though in ruins it remains an important part of India's archaeological and cultural heritage, because of what it was and what it left behind. (d) The student is wrong: even in the narrowest reading, from 600 CE to 1101 CE is 501 years, more than 300.
s: Part (a): a renowned centre of learning; the Sharada script
Part (b): Sharada Desh
Part (c): in ruins but part of archaeological and cultural heritage
Part (d): at least 501 years, so wrong

questions.q: Ishan reads that the chapter says temples grew into vast complexes 'from the 10th century onward' and that Rajaraja Chola I built the Brihadishvara Temple around 1010. He says: 'So it was built in the 10th century.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: The year 1010 falls in the 11th century, shortly after temples began growing into large complexes
o: The year 1010 falls in the 11th century, shortly after temples began growing into large complexes
The year 1010 falls in the 10th century, so the temple belongs to the very start of the growth in scale
The year 1010 falls in the 11th century, so the temple is older than the earlier modest temples
The year 1010 falls in the 9th century, since the modest temples of that time ended around then

questions.q: A conservator at Bishnupur is asked how an old terracotta panel was made. Which answer agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: First carved by hand, then fired in a kiln
o: First carved by hand, then fired in a kiln
First fired as a slab and then carved by hand once it had cooled down completely
Poured into a mould, set in the sun and then fixed on the wall
Cut from white marble, polished and then fired to harden it in a kiln

questions.q: Write a three-line description of an imaginary temple that shows how local material shapes a regional style. Use one of the chapter's examples of a locally sourced stone and one example of a brick structure, and label which example each part follows.
questions.a: Sample: 'The shrine in the hills is of white marble from the nearby range, carved on every surface, like the Dilwara Temples. The shrine on the plain is of brick, with square terracotta panels carved by hand and fired in a kiln, like Bishnupur's.' Labels: local stone (Dilwara's marble from the Aravalli hills, or Lingaraja's local sandstone and laterite); brick (Bishnupur's terracotta temples).
s: A stone temple tied to a nearby source, labelled
A brick or terracotta structure, labelled
The link that local material shapes the regional style

questions.q: (a) Who founded the Harmandir Sahib, and who continued the construction of the temple and its sarovar, and in which year? (b) The chapter calls the Harmandir Sahib the holiest of the Sikh shrines. A student says Guru Arjan Dev founded it. Correct him.
questions.a: (a) It was founded by Guru Ramdas Sahib, the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus; Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, continued the construction of the temple and its sarovar in 1588. (b) Guru Arjan Dev continued the work; the founder was Guru Ramdas Sahib.
s: Part (a): Guru Ramdas Sahib founded; Guru Arjan Dev continued in 1588
Part (b): the correction that Guru Ramdas Sahib was the founder

questions.q: A guide at Thanjavur tells visitors that the great Nandi was put together from many small granite blocks inside the main shrine. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: It is a massive statue carved from a single stone, in a pavilion facing the main shrine
o: It is a massive statue carved from a single stone, in a pavilion facing the main shrine
It is carved from a single stone, and stands inside the garbhagriha beside the deity of the temple
It is cast in terracotta, and sits in a pavilion facing the main shrine
It is built of many blocks of sandstone, and stands in the central mandapa

questions.q: (a) The Hidimba Devi Temple stands in Manali. Whom is it dedicated to, and in which century was it built? (b) What does the nearby temple dedicated to Ghatotkacha suggest, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) It is dedicated to Hidimba (Hirama), the wife of Bhima in the Mahabharata; it was built in the 16th century CE. (b) That the site has a close association with the epic tradition.
s: Part (a): Hidimba, wife of Bhima; 16th century CE
Part (b): close association with the epic tradition

questions.q: A guide at Mount Abu shares out 40 pilgrims equally among the separate Dilwara temples, so that each temple gets ___ pilgrims.
Maya says: 'The Lingaraja Temple and the Brihadishvara Temple are both dedicated to Shiva, and both are built entirely of granite.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Both temples are dedicated to Shiva, which is right. But the chapter says the Lingaraja Temple is built from locally available sandstone and laterite; granite is mentioned only for the carvings of the Brihadishvara Temple, so 'both entirely of granite' is wrong.
s: Right: both are dedicated to Shiva
Wrong: Lingaraja is of sandstone and laterite
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: Two imaginary builders plan temples. One has a hill of white marble nearby; the other has plenty of sandstone and laterite close by. Which pair of chapter temples did the same, using what their regions supplied?
questions.a: The Dilwara Temples, in white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills, and the Lingaraja Temple, in local sandstone and laterite
o: The Dilwara Temples, in white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills, and the Lingaraja Temple, in local sandstone and laterite
The Bishnupur temples, in marble from the Aravalli hills, and the Brihadishvara Temple, in sandstone and laterite
The Dilwara Temples, in terracotta panels fired in a kiln, and the Lingaraja Temple, in white marble
The Brihadishvara Temple, in white marble, and the Bishnupur temples, in locally available sandstone

questions.q: A tour operator can include only one of the Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur and the Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar in a short tour. For each requirement below, say which temple meets it or whether both do, with the chapter's evidence. (a) Dedicated to Shiva with secondary shrines for Parvati and other deities. (b) A vimana over 60 metres high. (c) Three large mandapas used for different purposes. (d) Built by Rajaraja Chola I. (e) Built from locally available sandstone and laterite.
questions.a: (a) Both: each is dedicated to Shiva, with several secondary shrines to goddess Parvati and other deities. (b) Brihadishvara: it has a huge vimana over 60 metres high. (c) Lingaraja: it has three large mandapas used for different purposes. (d) Brihadishvara: it was built by Rajaraja Chola I around 1010. (e) Lingaraja: it is built from locally available sandstone and laterite.
s: Part (a): both temples, with the evidence
Part (b): Brihadishvara
Part (c): Lingaraja
Part (d): Brihadishvara, built by Rajaraja Chola I
Part (e): Lingaraja

questions.q: Rohan notes: 'Sharada Peetha is a temple of Kashmir that still thrives with scholars.' (a) Correct his note about its present state. (b) State what the chapter says earned Kashmir the name Sharada Desh.
questions.a: (a) It is now in ruins, though it remains an important part of India's archaeological and cultural heritage; it flourished between the 6th and 12th centuries CE. (b) Its legacy as a renowned centre of learning dedicated to Goddess Sharada, and a key site in the development of the Sharada script, earned Kashmir the name Sharada Desh.
s: Part (a): now in ruins, having flourished from the 6th to the 12th centuries
Part (b): its legacy as a centre of learning earned the name

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says the Brihadishvara Temple is dedicated to Shiva and the Lingaraja Temple to Vishnu.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says both temples are dedicated to Shiva, each with several secondary shrines dedicated to goddess Parvati and other deities.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: both are dedicated to Shiva, with secondary shrines to Parvati and other deities

questions.q:
A class can make one trip only. The teacher's checklist has three equal needs: (i) carvings of Jain tirthankaras, (ii) ornamental patterns covering every surface, (iii) a temple built in the 17th or 18th century. She is choosing between the Dilwara Temples and the Bishnupur temples.
(a) Which needs does Dilwara meet, according to the chapter?
(b) Which needs does Bishnupur meet?
(c) Which site should the class visit, given that all three needs count equally?
(d) What material would the class see at the site you chose, and where does the chapter say it came from?
questions.a: (a) (i) and (ii): the carvings of Jain tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and ornamental patterns cover every surface. (b) (iii) only: Bishnupur's terracotta temples were built in the 17th and 18th centuries. (c) Dilwara: it meets two of the three needs and Bishnupur only one. (d) White marble, procured from the nearby Aravalli hills.
s: Part (a): needs (i) and (ii)
Part (b): need (iii) only
Part (c): Dilwara, two needs against one
Part (d): white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills

questions.q:
A restorer wants to rebuild the tops of the minarets of the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad. She has an 1809 sketch by a British army officer that shows full-size minarets, and a note saying the minarets of Delhi's Jama Masjid are 40 metres tall.
(a) What does the chapter say happened to the Ahmedabad minarets?
(b) What does the chapter say the 1809 sketch shows?
(c) Does the chapter give the height of the Ahmedabad minarets?
(d) She proposes to build them 40 metres tall, copying Delhi. Decide whether the chapter supports this.
questions.a: (a) The top portions were destroyed in earthquakes, leaving the bases on the facade. (b) The mosque's full-size minarets, so it shows what the top portions looked like. (c) No; the chapter gives 40 metres only for the two minarets of Delhi's Jama Masjid. (d) It does not support it: the 40 metres belongs to Delhi, the chapter gives no height for Ahmedabad's minarets, and the 1809 sketch is the source it points to for their full size.
s: Part (a): tops destroyed in earthquakes, bases remain
Part (b): the sketch shows the full-size minarets
Part (c): no height is given for Ahmedabad's minarets
Part (d): the 40 metres is Delhi's; use the sketch, not Delhi's figure

questions.q: (a) Name any two features of the Delhi Jama Masjid's scale that the chapter gives with numbers. (b) A planner of crowd arrangements has to choose between the number of workers who built it and the capacity of its courtyard. Which should she use, and what is it?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: about 5,000 workers pressed into service; minarets 40 metres tall; a courtyard for up to 25,000 people; three large domes or three large entrances. (b) The courtyard capacity, up to 25,000 people, since it states how many people it can hold.
s: Part (a): any two numbered features
Part (b): the courtyard capacity of up to 25,000 people

questions.q: (a) Which prayers does the chapter call especially important in Islam? (b) Using (a), explain why a large mosque such as the one Shah Jahan built in Delhi is called a Jama Masjid.
questions.a: (a) The Friday prayers. (b) Large mosques where the Friday prayers are held are often called Jama Masjid; jama means gathering or assembly and masjid means mosque, so the name is 'the mosque of gathering', fitting Shah Jahan's vision of a mosque where the city's Muslims could gather for prayer.
s: Part (a): the Friday prayers
Part (b): jama means gathering or assembly, masjid mosque, so a mosque for large gatherings

questions.q:
On a Friday the courtyard of the Jama Masjid in Delhi is expected to hold 18,400 worshippers (an illustrative figure). Two groups ask to use the courtyard for an event on the same occasion: Group B expects 7,500 people and Group C expects 6,000.
(a) Using the capacity the chapter gives, how many more people can the courtyard hold?
(b) By how many would Group B exceed it?
(c) How many places would remain if Group C were admitted?
(d) Decide which group can be admitted.
questions.a: (a) 25,000 - 18,400 = 6,600. (b) 7,500 - 6,600 = 900 more than the courtyard can hold. (c) 6,600 - 6,000 = 600 places. (d) Group C: it fits within the capacity of up to 25,000, while Group B would exceed it by 900.
s: Part (b): exceeds by 900
Part (c): 600 places remain
Part (d): Group C

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Shah Jahan built the Jama Masjid in Delhi after moving his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad.
Reason (R): A mosque has a prayer hall oriented towards Mecca.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The chapter says scholars 'suggest' local Hindu and Jain artisans helped build the Ahmedabad Jama Masjid. (a) Name three observations that led them to this. (b) Why is 'suggest' a careful word? (c) What general feature of Indo-Islamic architecture does it illustrate?
questions.a: (a) The intricate stone jalis, pillars in the same style as some temples (but without decorations) and some detailed carvings. (b) No record of the craftsmen is quoted in the chapter; the scholars are reading the buildings' features, so the conclusion is an inference. (c) That Indo-Islamic architecture blends Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship.
s: Part (a): jalis, temple-style pillars and detailed carvings
Part (b): it is an inference from features, not a recorded fact
Part (c): blending of Islamic traditions with Indian craftsmanship

questions.q: A guide at the Jama Masjid in Delhi says: 'Akbar built it in the mid-17th century after moving his capital from Delhi to Agra.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: Shah Jahan, mid-17th century, after moving his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad
o: Shah Jahan, mid-17th century, after moving his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad
Shah Jahan, in the 15th century, after moving his capital from Agra to Delhi itself as a new city
Sultan Ahmed Shah I, in the mid-17th century, after moving his capital to Shahjahanabad
Akbar, in the mid-17th century, after moving his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad

questions.q: A town committee plans a new large mosque for Friday prayers. (a) How must its prayer hall be oriented, and which niche in the wall marks the direction? (b) What should stand on either side of the domes, and for what purpose? (c) The committee also wants to hold classes and public lectures there. Does the chapter's account allow this? (d) By what name may such a mosque be called, and what does the name mean?
questions.a: (a) Towards Mecca, the most sacred site in Islam; the niche that points to that direction is the mihrab. (b) Minarets (towers), from which the muezzin makes the call to prayer. (c) Yes: the chapter says mosques also serve as centres for religious education and community gatherings, and as venues for lectures and discussions. (d) A Jama Masjid, since large mosques where the Friday prayers are held are often so called; jama means gathering or assembly and masjid means mosque.
s: Part (a): oriented towards Mecca
Part (a): the mihrab
Part (b): minarets for the muezzin's call to prayer
Part (c): yes; education, gatherings, lectures and discussions
Part (d): Jama Masjid, 'mosque of gathering'

questions.q: Write a three-line description of an imaginary mosque in Rajasthan that has the chapter's features of Indo-Islamic architecture and also local Rajasthani features. Label each feature you name.
questions.a: Sample: 'A prayer hall with a dome and pointed arches faces Mecca, and jalis let in air. Floral motifs run along its walls. Ornate jharokhas and chhatris crown the facade.' Labels: dome, pointed arches, jalis and floral motifs are Indo-Islamic features; jharokhas (overhanging balconies) and chhatris (pavilion domes) are the Rajasthani features the chapter says were integrated.
s: Two or more Indo-Islamic features named and labelled
Jharokhas and chhatris as local Rajasthani features
A sensible description joining the two

questions.q: Dev says: 'The chapter proves that the Ahmedabad Jama Masjid was built entirely by Hindu and Jain craftsmen, who alone planned it.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says only that the jalis, temple-style pillars and carvings have led scholars to suggest that the mosque was constructed with the help of local Hindu and Jain artisans, masons and stone carvers. That is a suggestion, not proof; it says 'with the help of', not 'entirely by', and it says nothing of who planned it.
s: The chapter only says scholars suggest it, which is not proof
'With the help of', not 'entirely by' or 'alone planned'
Verdict: No

questions.q:
Read the statements about mosques.
1. The mihrab is the niche in the wall that points towards Mecca.
2. The Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad is of yellow sandstone and blends Hindu and Islamic architectural elements.
3. The courtyard of the Jama Masjid in Delhi can accommodate up to 2,500 people.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Define 'Indo-Islamic architecture' as the chapter does, and name two of its features.
questions.a: It is architecture that blends Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship. Two of its features: domes, arches (pointed or corbelled), jalis, floral motifs.
s: Definition: a blend of Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship
Two features from the chapter's list

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the architectural term in Column B.
Column A: 1. A latticed screen that lets air and light through a window.  2. An overhanging balcony.  3. A pavilion dome.  4. The niche in a mosque wall that points towards Mecca.
Column B: a. mihrab  b. jali  c. chhatri  d. jharokha
True or False? 'The chapter says the Ahmedabad Jama Masjid blends Hindu and Islamic elements, and that the tops of its minarets were destroyed in earthquakes.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the structure of yellow sandstone has a blend of Hindu and Islamic architectural elements, and that the top portions of the two minarets were destroyed in earthquakes, as an 1809 sketch with full-size minarets shows.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a blend of Hindu and Islamic elements; minaret tops destroyed in earthquakes, seen in the 1809 sketch

questions.q: (a) What is a minaret, and what is it used for in a large mosque, according to the chapter? (b) Using (a), say where the minarets stand in relation to the domes.
questions.a: (a) A minaret is a tower, from which the muezzin makes the call to prayer. (b) Minarets stand on either side of the domes.
s: Part (a): a tower from which the muezzin calls to prayer
Part (b): on either side of the domes

questions.q: A mason spans a doorway by stacking blocks so that each layer juts out slightly beyond the one below, like a staircase turned upside down, until the two sides meet. Which feature from the chapter's list of Indo-Islamic features names this method?
questions.a: A corbelled arch made of stacked blocks
o: A corbelled arch made of stacked blocks
A pointed arch made of blocks that lean inward
A jharokha balcony of carved stone that overhangs a street
A chhatri pavilion

questions.q: A builder in a distant town is fitting the niche in the wall of a new mosque's prayer hall. Which direction must the niche, the mihrab, point to?
questions.a: The direction of Mecca, the most sacred site in Islam, towards which the whole prayer hall is oriented
o: The direction of Mecca, the most sacred site in Islam, towards which the whole prayer hall is oriented
The direction of sunrise, as the call to prayer is made at dawn
The direction of the town's largest Jama Masjid
The direction in which the minarets stand beside the domes

questions.q: A city's biggest mosque, where the Friday prayers draw the whole community, is called its Jama Masjid. Which explanation matches the chapter?
questions.a: Large mosques where Friday prayers are held are often so called, jama meaning gathering
o: Large mosques where Friday prayers are held are often so called, jama meaning gathering
It is the oldest mosque of a city, with jama meaning ancient in the language of the builders
It is a mosque built by a sultan, with jama meaning royal in the language of the court
It is a mosque with latticed screens, with jama meaning lattice

questions.q: The red-stone courtyard of Delhi's Jama Masjid is filled to the limit the chapter gives and the people are divided into groups of 50. The number of groups is ___.
Show that the claim 'Shah Jahan built the Jama Masjid in Delhi while Agra was still his capital' cannot be supported by the chapter.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says Shah Jahan built the Jama Masjid in the mid-17th century. (2) It says he did so after he moved his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (now Old Delhi). (3) So the mosque followed the move; it was not built while Agra was still the capital.
s: Mosque built in the mid-17th century by Shah Jahan
Built after the capital moved from Agra to Shahjahanabad
So it was not built while Agra was the capital

questions.q: A visitor to Delhi's Jama Masjid says: 'The whole mosque is made of white marble.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: It is made of red sandstone with white marble decorations
o: It is made of red sandstone with white marble decorations
It is made of yellow sandstone, a blend of Hindu and Islamic elements, with white marble only for its minarets
It is made of red sandstone only, and its only decoration is the calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an
It is made of white marble below and red sandstone above, with a courtyard paved in sandstone

questions.q: A guide has to say, for each feature below, whether the chapter ties it to the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad, to that of Delhi, or to both. (a) Yellow sandstone. (b) About 5,000 workers pressed into service. (c) Tops of the minarets destroyed in earthquakes. (d) Walls and arches decorated with calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an. (e) A blend of Hindu and Islamic architectural elements.
questions.a: (a) Ahmedabad: the structure is of yellow sandstone. (b) Delhi. (c) Ahmedabad: the top portions of its two minarets were destroyed in earthquakes. (d) Delhi: the walls and arches are decorated with calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an. (e) Ahmedabad: it has a blend of Hindu and Islamic architectural elements.
s: Part (a): Ahmedabad
Part (b): Delhi
Part (c): Ahmedabad
Part (d): Delhi
Part (e): Ahmedabad

questions.q: The red sandstone of Agra's Red Fort was mined at Dholpur. At the distance the chapter gives, a cart that covers 15 km a day (an illustrative speed) would take ___ days to bring one load.

A builder says: 'Jodhpur's houses near the fort are blue because blue reflects the sun, and that is what keeps them cool.'
(a) What does the chapter say the blue colour is made from, and what is it said to do?
(b) Judge the builder's claim.
(c) Name three features the chapter lists as working together to keep the houses cool.
(d) A new colony copies only the blue wash on thin-walled houses without jali windows or courtyards. Predict, from the chapter, whether it will be as cool as Jodhpur's houses.
questions.a: (a) A solution of copper sulphate mixed with lime, said to repel termites. (b) Not supported: the chapter gives the blue wash as a termite repellent, not as the reason for coolness. (c) Any three of: meandering streets, open courtyards, jali windows for ventilation, thick walls, balconies. (d) Probably not: the chapter says the cooling features work together, and the colony would have none of them, only the wash.
s: Part (a): copper sulphate and lime; said to repel termites
Part (b): the chapter does not give the blue as the reason for coolness
Part (c): three cooling features
Part (d): not as cool, since the cooling features are missing

questions.q: The chapter says forts and palaces are 'clubbed together'. (a) What did forts protect? (b) Who lived in them? (c) How do (a) and (b) explain why the two categories are treated together?
questions.a: (a) They protected a kingdom from the onslaught of invaders. (b) The ruling and military classes lived in forts, and in some cases an entire city, and some forts also sheltered a royal palace. (c) Because some forts also sheltered a royal palace, the two categories overlap, so the chapter treats them together.
s: Part (a): protection of a kingdom from invaders
Part (b): residences of the ruling and military classes, sometimes a city, and some had a palace
Part (c): since some forts sheltered a palace, the two are treated together

questions.q: Show that the claim 'the red sandstone of Agra's Red Fort was quarried right next to the fort' cannot be supported by the chapter.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says the fort's name comes from the red sandstone. (2) It says that this stone was mined at Dholpur in Rajasthan. (3) It puts Dholpur some 60 km from Agra, so the stone was brought from a distance, not quarried beside the fort.
s: The fort's name comes from its red sandstone
The stone was mined at Dholpur in Rajasthan
Dholpur is some 60 km away

questions.q: Compare the fort Akbar rebuilt at Agra with what Shah Jahan did to it, on materials used.
questions.a: Akbar rebuilt a brick fort that had fallen to ruin, in red sandstone, which gave the fort its name. Shah Jahan, fond of marble, replaced many of the sandstone buildings, particularly the palaces, with marble ones.
s: Akbar: red sandstone rebuilding of a ruined brick fort
Shah Jahan: marble replacing many sandstone palaces

questions.q: Zoya says: 'The Mehrangarh Fort was begun in the mid-15th century, Rajput rulers kept expanding it for about two centuries, and parts of it are now a museum.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says construction began in the mid-15th century, that Rajput rulers continued to expand it over the next two centuries or so, and that many parts of the fort have been converted into a museum to preserve and showcase the fort's and Rajasthan's cultural heritage.
s: Begun in the mid-15th century
Expanded by Rajput rulers over about two centuries
Now partly a museum; verdict: yes

questions.q:
A palace planner wants cooling fountains for a courtyard and compares two plans (illustrative figures). Plan 1 copies the system of Agra's Red Fort: a Persian wheel lifts river water into overhead tanks on the walls and terracotta pipes carry it down to the fountains; it costs Rs 6 lakh once and nothing a year to run. Plan 2 uses an electric pump: Rs 3 lakh once and Rs 1.5 lakh a year.
(a) Describe, in order, how water reaches the fountains in the Agra system.
(b) What would each plan cost over 10 years?
(c) After how many years do the two plans cost the same?
(d) The palace is meant to last far beyond 10 years. Decide which plan to adopt, and give the chapter's word for the Agra system.
questions.a: (a) Water from the Yamuna was lifted by Persian wheels into overhead tanks on the walls; from the tanks it flowed down through terracotta pipes to create fountains. (b) Plan 1: Rs 6 lakh. Plan 2: 3 + 1.5 x 10 = Rs 18 lakh. (c) 3 + 1.5n = 6 gives n = 2 years. (d) Plan 1: after 2 years it is the cheaper, and over 10 years it costs Rs 12 lakh less; the chapter calls such fountains eco-friendly 'air-conditioners'.
s: Part (a): Persian wheels, overhead tanks, then terracotta pipes
Part (b): Rs 6 lakh against Rs 18 lakh
Part (c): 2 years
Part (d): Plan 1, with 'eco-friendly air-conditioners'

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The fountains of Agra's Red Fort worked as eco-friendly 'air-conditioners'.
Reason (R): The fountains, made by water flowing down terracotta pipes from overhead tanks, helped keep the area cool.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A council must choose a site for a new fort. Site 1 is a hilltop beside an important trade road, with a view of the plains. Site 2 is a valley floor beside a river, 30 km from any road. Site 3 is a plain beside the capital's market. (a) Which site does the chapter's reasoning favour, and with which two reasons? (b) Say what is wrong with each of the other two sites on the chapter's reasoning. (c) The king wants his household and soldiers inside. Name three kinds of occupants or buildings the chapter says forts held. (d) Name one chapter fort whose palace had quarters for several groups, and give two of them.
questions.a: (a) Site 1: forts were strategically located near important land or sea routes, and often atop a hill so as to command a view of the plains below. (b) Site 2 is far from any route and low, so it has no view of the plains; Site 3 lies on a plain with no height to command a view. (c) Residences of the ruling and military classes, in some cases an entire city, and in some cases a royal palace. (d) Mehrangarh: any two of areas for royalty, separate quarters for men and women, living quarters for staff, stables and barracks.
s: Part (a): Site 1 with two reasons (route and hilltop view)
Part (b): why Sites 2 and 3 fail on those reasons
Part (c): three kinds of occupants or buildings
Part (d): Mehrangarh
Part (d): two of its quarters

questions.q: A guide at a heritage meet must match each feature to the right place among Mehrangarh at Jodhpur, the Red Fort at Agra, the Orchha complex and the Mysuru Palace. (a) Rebuilt early in the 20th century after a wooden palace was destroyed by fire. (b) Three main palaces: Raja Mahal, Jahangir Mahal and Rai Praveen Mahal, on the banks of the Betwa. (c) Many of its buildings destroyed by British troops of the East India Company in the 19th century. (d) A memorial to Maharaja Jaswant Singh II built nearby. (e) A golden throne displayed during the Dasara festival.
questions.a: (a) Mysuru Palace. (b) The Orchha Fort-Palace complex. (c) The Red Fort at Agra. (d) Mehrangarh at Jodhpur (the Jaswant Thada). (e) Mysuru Palace.
s: Part (a): Mysuru Palace
Part (b): Orchha
Part (c): Agra Red Fort
Part (d): Mehrangarh, the Jaswant Thada
Part (e): Mysuru Palace

questions.q: Write a three-line description of an imaginary hill fort that shows both purposes the chapter gives for forts, defence and housing. Label which line shows which.
questions.a: Sample: 'The fort stands on a hilltop beside the trade road, with a view over the plains. Inside its walls lie the king's palace, soldiers' barracks and stables. Houses for the court's servants fill the lower terraces.' Labels: first line, defence by site; later lines, residences of the ruling and military classes.
s: A site chosen for defence, such as hilltop near a route, labelled
Residences of the ruling or military classes inside the fort, labelled
A coherent three-line description

questions.q: True or False? 'The Jahangir Mahal at Orchha was built to commemorate Emperor Jahangir's visit, and it blends Rajput and Mughal architectural styles.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the Jahangir Mahal, one of the three main palaces of the Orchha complex built by the Bundela Rajput kings, was built to commemorate Emperor Jahangir's visit and showcases a blend of Rajput and Mughal styles.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: built to commemorate Jahangir's visit, and a blend of Rajput and Mughal styles

questions.q: A king in an imaginary kingdom wants a fort that will protect his lands from invaders. Which site would the chapter's reasoning favour?
questions.a: A hilltop near an important land route, with a view of the plains below
o: A hilltop near an important land route, with a view of the plains below
A river valley far from any road, hidden from the plains around it
A low site in the plain beside the market, so that traders can enter easily
A forest clearing between two villages, shielded by dense trees all around

questions.q: (a) What is a cenotaph? (b) Using (a), explain why the chapter says the Jaswant Thada is not a tomb.
questions.a: (a) A monument in the memory of a historical figure, at a spot where the person is not buried. (b) The Maharaja it remembers was not buried there; it served as the cremation ground for Jodhpur's royal family, so it is a cenotaph and not a tomb.
s: Part (a): a monument in memory of a person who is not buried at the spot
Part (b): the deceased is not buried there, so it is not a tomb

questions.q:
Read the statements about forts and palaces.
1. Forts were strategically located near important land or sea routes, and often atop a hill.
2. Agra's Red Fort was originally built of marble, which Akbar later replaced with sandstone.
3. The Orchha complex was built by the Wadiyar kings on the banks of the Betwa.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A historian describes a very large fort in which the ruling family, the army and many townspeople all lived within the same walls. Which statement from the chapter does this fit?
questions.a: Forts accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes and, depending on their size, even an entire city
o: Forts accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes and, depending on their size, even an entire city
Forts were built only on plains, and the townspeople lived outside, away from the soldiers
Forts housed only palaces, while the military classes lived in separate cenotaph complexes
Forts always held a royal palace, so that the two categories were never treated separately

questions.q: An architect wants houses in a hot town to stay cool without machines, and takes hints from Jodhpur's traditional houses near the fort. Which set of features does the chapter list as working together to keep them cool?
questions.a: Jali windows for ventilation, thick walls, balconies, open courtyards and meandering streets
o: Jali windows for ventilation, thick walls, balconies, open courtyards and meandering streets
Thin walls, sealed windows, flat roofs and a blue coat of copper sulphate and lime on the walls
Marble facing, a single large door, straight wide streets and tall narrow rooms
A copper sulphate and lime coat on the walls, which the chapter says cools the rooms

questions.q: On the bank of a river in Madhya Pradesh a visitor sees parasol-shaped cenotaphs near a fort-palace complex of three main palaces, linked to a famous temple. Which complex is it?
questions.a: Orchha, on the banks of the river Betwa
o: Orchha, on the banks of the river Betwa
Mehrangarh, whose cenotaph, the Jaswant Thada, stands in the foreground of the fort
Agra's Red Fort, whose palaces of marble overlook the Yamuna and are linked to the Taj Mahal
The Mysuru Palace, whose golden throne is shown during the Dasara festival every year

questions.q: (a) Describe in order how water reached the fountains of Agra's Red Fort. (b) Why does the chapter call the fountains eco-friendly?
questions.a: (a) Water from the Yamuna was lifted by Persian wheels into overhead tanks on the walls; from the tanks it flowed down through terracotta pipes to create the fountains. (b) They helped keep the area cool as 'air-conditioners' without machines, using lifted water and terracotta pipes.
s: Part (a): Persian wheels to overhead tanks, then terracotta pipes to fountains
Part (b): kept the area cool as eco-friendly air-conditioners

questions.q: A tourist at the Mysuru Palace says: 'This wooden palace has stood unchanged since the Wadiyars first built it.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The present structure was built early in the 20th century, after the previous wooden palace was destroyed by fire
o: The present structure was built early in the 20th century, after the previous wooden palace was destroyed by fire
The present structure was built in the 15th century, after the previous palace fell to ruin from neglect
The present structure was built by Akbar, after a fire destroyed the earlier palace of the dynasty
The present structure was built in the mid-17th century, after the royal family moved its capital

questions.q: (a) Name two kinds of rooms or spaces that the chapter lists inside the Mehrangarh palace. (b) Using (a), say what this shows about a fort beyond defence.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: areas for the royalty, separate quarters for men and women, living quarters for the staff, stables and barracks. (b) That a fort also housed a household, the ruler's family, staff and soldiers, as the chapter says forts accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes.
s: Part (a): two spaces from the chapter's list
Part (b): forts also housed the ruling and military classes

questions.q: Asha says: 'In Islam, mausoleums were built for rulers and also for renowned mystics, and Hindu rulers in ancient India were buried in tombs as well.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: in the Islamic world mausoleums were often built for prominent rulers, members of the royal household or renowned mystics. The second half is wrong: in Hinduism the dead are generally cremated, and no tombs of rulers of such faiths exist in India in ancient times.
s: First half right: rulers, royal household and renowned mystics
Second half wrong: Hindu dead are generally cremated; no ancient tombs
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
A designer wants a new monument to echo the Taj Mahal's 'confluence of architectural styles from three cultures'. Three briefs are submitted.
Brief A: charbagh gardens, large arched doorways, Arabic calligraphy from the Qur'an, chhatris, lotus flower designs and marble screens with cutout patterns.
Brief B: charbagh gardens, large arched doorways and calligraphy from the Qur'an.
Brief C: chhatris, lotus flower designs and marble screens with cutout patterns.
(a) Which brief reproduces all three cultures?
(b) Which culture does Brief B lack, and which features would supply it?
(c) Which cultures does Brief C lack?
(d) Name one decorative technique on the Taj's walls, using semi-precious stones, that none of the briefs mentions.
questions.a: (a) Brief A. (b) Indian; chhatris, lotus flower designs and marble screens with detailed cutout patterns. (c) Persian (charbagh gardens, large arched doorways) and Arabic (calligraphy from the Qur'an). (d) Inlay work: colourful semi-precious stones embedded in the marble to create floral designs.
s: Part (a): Brief A
Part (b): Indian, with its three features
Part (c): Persian and Arabic
Part (d): inlay of semi-precious stones in floral designs

questions.q: (a) Describe the inlay work on the walls of the Taj Mahal. (b) Using (a), name which of the three cultures the chapter credits for the marble screens with cutout patterns, and which for the calligraphy from the Qur'an.
questions.a: (a) Craftsmen embedded colourful semi-precious stones into the marble to create floral designs. (b) Indian architecture added the marble screens with detailed cutout patterns; the calligraphy from the Qur'an is Arabic.
s: Part (a): semi-precious stones set in marble in floral designs
Part (b): marble screens Indian; calligraphy from the Qur'an Arabic

questions.q: A guide at Delhi sorts the features of two monuments for a quiz. For each, say whether it belongs to Humayun's Tomb, to the Taj Mahal, or to neither as the chapter describes them. (a) Commissioned by the chief wife of the ruler it houses. (b) Designed by Persian architects. (c) Charbagh gardens of Persian inspiration. (d) Houses the tombs of several Mughals, including Dara Shikoh. (e) Walls with inlay of colourful semi-precious stones in floral designs.
questions.a: (a) Humayun's Tomb: commissioned by Humayun's chief wife, Bega Begum, in 1558. (b) Humayun's Tomb: designed by Persian architects. (c) The Taj Mahal: the chapter names the charbagh gardens among its Persian features. (d) Humayun's Tomb: the complex houses the tombs of several Mughals, including Dara Shikoh. (e) The Taj Mahal: its walls have delicate inlay work.
s: Part (a): Humayun's Tomb
Part (b): Humayun's Tomb
Part (c): the Taj Mahal
Part (d): Humayun's Tomb
Part (e): the Taj Mahal

questions.q:
Read the statements about tombs and mausoleums.
1. Humayun's Tomb was designed by Indian architects and commissioned by Shah Jahan.
2. The Taj Mahal was built in the mid-16th century by Akbar.
3. In Islam and in Christianity the dead are buried.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says Humayun's Tomb complex houses only Humayun's own tomb.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the complex also houses the tombs of several Mughals, including that of Dara Shikoh.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it houses the tombs of several Mughals, including Dara Shikoh

questions.q: (a) Who commissioned Humayun's Tomb, and when? (b) Using (a), say what the architects' origin added to the Mughal architectural tradition.
questions.a: (a) Humayun's chief wife, Bega Begum, in 1558. (b) The architects were Persian; they brought Persian aesthetics that became part of the Mughal architectural tradition.
s: Part (a): Bega Begum, Humayun's chief wife, in 1558
Part (b): Persian architects brought Persian aesthetics into the Mughal tradition

questions.q:
A city's white marble monument has turned yellowish. Three causes are suggested: A, weather; B, the breath of crowds of visitors; C, local industries burning coal and other fossil fuels. A councillor asks what the chapter's example of the Taj Mahal suggests.
(a) Which cause does the chapter's example support, and what kind of pollution was it?
(b) In which decade did the effect begin to be noticed?
(c) Which two things came before the ban?
(d) Predict, from the chapter's example, what step the city should aim for if it finds cause C to be true.
questions.a: (a) Cause C: air pollution caused by local industries using coal and other fossil fuels, which left a yellowish tinge on the marble. (b) The 1970s. (c) The recommendations of an expert committee and a PIL in the Supreme Court. (d) A ban on industrial pollution in the area, as was imposed in the mid-1990s at the Taj Mahal.
s: Part (a): cause C, air pollution from coal and fossil fuels
Part (b): the 1970s
Part (c): expert committee and a PIL in the Supreme Court
Part (d): a ban on industrial pollution in the area

questions.q: A scholar notes that some larger mosques and the mausoleums described in the chapter share certain features. Which set does the chapter name as common?
questions.a: Arches, floral motifs, latticework and calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an
o: Arches, floral motifs, latticework and calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an
Minarets, a mihrab, domes and a muezzin's gallery, as in every large mosque
Charbagh gardens, chhatris, jharokhas and corbelled arches, as in every mausoleum
Jalis, white marble inlay, a courtyard for thousands and two tall minarets, as in Delhi

questions.q: Write a three-line description of an imaginary mausoleum for a ruler that follows the chapter's account of mausoleums: its purpose, its layout and two common features. Label each line.
questions.a: Sample: 'The grand tomb houses the ruler and his family and stands as a statement of the dynasty's greatness. Its plan is strictly symmetrical and the symmetry extends to the gardens around it. Its walls carry arches and calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an.' Labels: purpose (a political statement and burial place), symmetry extending to gardens, two common features (arches, calligraphy; also floral motifs, latticework).
s: A purpose: housing tombs and a statement of dynastic greatness
Strict symmetry extending to gardens
Two common features, such as arches, floral motifs, latticework or calligraphy

questions.q: A visitor photographs the Taj Mahal at 9 a.m. and again at 4 p.m. and says the marble looks different. (a) What does the chapter say about the colour of the white marble, and why? (b) The visitor looks closely at the walls. Which decoration of colourful stones will she see? (c) She asks what mix of cultures the building shows; name one feature from each. (d) She notices a yellowish tinge in an old photograph from the 1970s. What was its cause, and what did the city do about it by the mid-1990s?
questions.a: (a) The white marble appears to change colours as the sunlight shifts through the day. (b) Inlay work: colourful semi-precious stones embedded in the marble to create floral designs. (c) Persian: charbagh gardens or large arched doorways; Arabic: calligraphy from the Qur'an; Indian: chhatris, lotus flower designs or marble screens. (d) Air pollution from local industries using coal and other fossil fuels; after an expert committee's recommendations and a PIL in the Supreme Court, a ban on industrial pollution in the area was imposed in the mid-1990s.
s: Part (a): the colour appears to change as sunlight shifts
Part (b): inlay of semi-precious stones in floral designs
Part (c): one feature from each of three cultures
Part (d): coal and fossil-fuel pollution from local industries
Part (d): the mid-1990s ban after committee and PIL

questions.q: A charbagh garden of 3,600 square metres (an illustrative figure) is laid out as the chapter says charbagh gardens are divided, into equal sections. Each section covers ___ square metres.
A student sorts the features of the Taj Mahal by the culture the chapter links them to. Which sorting matches the chapter?
questions.a: Persian: charbagh gardens, arched doorways; Arabic: calligraphy; Indian: chhatris, lotus designs
o: Persian: charbagh gardens, arched doorways; Arabic: calligraphy; Indian: chhatris, lotus designs
Persian: calligraphy from the Qur'an; Arabic: charbagh gardens, arched doorways; Indian: chhatris, lotus designs, marble screens
Persian: chhatris, lotus designs, marble screens; Arabic: charbagh gardens; Indian: calligraphy from the Qur'an, arched doorways
Persian: marble screens, lotus designs; Arabic: chhatris; Indian: charbagh gardens, arched doorways, calligraphy

questions.q: A guide says: 'The six-pointed star on Humayun's Tomb is a purely Islamic symbol.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: It is found in several traditions: the Star of David, the Seal of Solomon and a Hindu tantric symbol
o: It is found in several traditions: the Star of David, the Seal of Solomon and a Hindu tantric symbol
It belongs to Islam, where it is named the Seal of Solomon, and to no other tradition of the world at all
It is Persian, brought by the architects, and the traditions of India never used it in any form
It is found in Judaism and Islam, but Hindu tantric symbolism has a different one altogether

questions.q: Show that the Taj Mahal cannot be described as a purely Persian building, using the chapter.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says the Taj Mahal is a confluence of architectural styles from three cultures. (2) Persian inspiration appears in the charbagh gardens and the large arched doorways, while Arabic calligraphy from the Qur'an adorns the walls. (3) Indian architecture added chhatris, lotus designs and marble screens, so features of three cultures are present, not only the Persian.
s: A confluence of three cultures' styles
Persian and Arabic features named
Indian features named, so not purely Persian

questions.q: In an imaginary Rajasthan town, a stone memorial stands where a king's brother was cremated. Nobody is buried there. What does the chapter call such a monument, and when does it say such monuments appeared?
questions.a: A cenotaph, which appeared in the medieval era, especially in Rajasthan and central India
o: A cenotaph, which appeared in the medieval era, especially in Rajasthan and central India
A mausoleum, which appeared in the medieval era, especially in Rajasthan and central India
A cenotaph, which appeared in ancient times, especially in Buddhist and Jain traditions
A tomb, which appeared in ancient times, especially in the Islamic world

questions.q:
Assertion (A): No tombs of rulers of the Buddhist, Jain or Hindu faiths exist in India from ancient times.
Reason (R): In Buddhism, Jainism and Hinduism the dead are generally cremated.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A visitor says the Taj Mahal was built for Shah Jahan's mother in brick, in the 15th century. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: It is a marble mausoleum for his queen Mumtaz Mahal, built in the mid-17th century
o: It is a marble mausoleum for his queen Mumtaz Mahal, built in the mid-17th century
It is a marble mausoleum for his queen Mumtaz Mahal, built in the mid-16th century by Akbar
It is a red sandstone mausoleum for Shah Jahan himself, built in the mid-17th century
It is a marble mosque for his queen Mumtaz Mahal, built in the mid-17th century

questions.q: (a) The chapter calls mausoleums 'a political statement'. What did they stand as a testament to? (b) Using (a), explain why they were often built for prominent rulers.
questions.a: (a) The greatness of the royalty or their dynasty. (b) A grand building for a prominent ruler told everyone how great the ruler and the dynasty were, so such buildings served as a statement of power as well as a place of burial.
s: Part (a): a testament to the greatness of the royalty or their dynasty
Part (b): grand tombs for rulers announced the dynasty's greatness

questions.q: Differentiate a tomb from a cenotaph, using what the chapter says about burial and cremation.
questions.a: A tomb houses a person who has been buried, as in Islam and Christianity; a cenotaph is a monument in memory of someone who is not buried at the spot, and in India it marked only the place where a king or family member was cremated.
s: A tomb: where the dead are buried
A cenotaph: a memorial where the person is not buried; it marked a place of cremation

questions.q:
Match each description of the six-pointed star in Column A with what it refers to in Column B.
Column A: 1. In Judaism, named after a king of the Hebrews.  2. In Islam, named after a king regarded as a model king and a prophet.  3. In Hindu tantric symbolism, the upward-pointing triangle.  4. In Hindu tantric symbolism, the downward-pointing triangle.
Column B: a. Prakriti or shakti  b. Seal of Solomon  c. Star of David  d. Purusha or consciousness
A visitor notes four features of Kerala churches. Which pair does the chapter say comes from local architectural traditions?
questions.a: A stambha (flag post) in front, borrowed from temple architecture, and a sloped tiled roof
o: A stambha (flag post) in front, borrowed from temple architecture, and a sloped tiled roof
Pointed arches and large windows with stained glass, from the Gothic style
Domes and minarets on either side, taken over from mosques
A tower above the inner chamber and a gopuram

questions.q:
A citizens' group has Rs 6 lakh (illustrative figures) and can use it on one monument only. Monument P is a well-known palace with an annual maintenance budget of Rs 40 lakh from a government body. Monument Q is a lesser-known old temple whose failing roof needs Rs 5 lakh to be saved; it has no caretaker and no budget.
(a) How much of the Rs 6 lakh would remain after saving Q's roof?
(b) What percentage of P's budget is the whole Rs 6 lakh?
(c) Which remark from the chapter's closing section describes Q's situation?
(d) Decide which monument should receive the money.
questions.a: (a) 6 - 5 = Rs 1 lakh. (b) 6 / 40 x 100 = 15 per cent. (c) That anyone visiting lesser-known monuments will notice that many are in a state of neglect. (d) Monument Q: the fund fully covers its roof, whereas it would add only 15 per cent to P's existing budget; Q is also the kind of neglected, lesser-known monument the chapter worries about.
s: Part (a): Rs 1 lakh
Part (b): 15 per cent
Part (c): many lesser-known monuments are in a state of neglect
Part (d): Q, with the figures as support

questions.q: (a) What design is common in traditional houses of the richer classes, according to the chapter? (b) Using (a), say what some archaeologists have remarked about its age.
questions.a: (a) A central courtyard with the rooms organised around it, over one or several storeys, in both urban and rural contexts. (b) That the design was already in use in some of the larger Harappan houses some 4,500 years ago.
s: Part (a): a central courtyard with rooms organised around it
Part (b): already in use in some larger Harappan houses some 4,500 years ago

questions.q: A court building completed in 1892 during the British Raj has a red sandstone facade with Islamic arches and intricate screens alongside carvings and pillars in Hindu temple style. Which style does the chapter place it in?
questions.a: Indo-Saracenic, a colonial style blending Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements
o: Indo-Saracenic, a colonial style blending Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements
Indo-Islamic, a style that blends Islamic traditions with Indian craftsmanship alone
Gothic, a European style with pointed arches and stained-glass windows
Classical temple style, shaped by the principles of the shilpashastra

questions.q: (a) Quote or paraphrase the Fundamental Duty the chapter cites. (b) Using (a), explain why the chapter says that 'citizens' as well as government bodies must act.
questions.a: (a) 'To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.' (b) A duty applies to every citizen; the chapter says that government bodies are only theoretically responsible for the huge task of conserving thousands of monuments and much will be lost unless citizens feel equally responsible.
s: Part (a): to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
Part (b): the task is too large for government bodies alone; citizens must feel equally responsible

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chettinadu houses are known for being well adapted to the local climate and environment.
Reason (R): Teakwood from Burma and marble from Italy were used in building them.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Compare Shekhawati havelis and Chettinadu houses. Give (a) who owned each kind, (b) one decoration or artistic feature of each, and (c) one feature they share.
questions.a: (a) Havelis were homes of Shekhawati's nobility and rich merchant class; Chettinadu houses belonged to a community of merchants who traded in rice, spices and gems with Southeast Asia. (b) Havelis: painted frescoes; Chettinadu: frescoes by craftsmen from all over India, or decorated woodwork and pillars. (c) Both have a central courtyard, and both are almost like palaces in size and artistry.
s: Part (a): owners of each
Part (b): one artistic feature of each
Part (c): the shared central courtyard

questions.q: A student says: 'Indo-Saracenic architecture is just Mughal architecture with a few Rajput touches.' Evaluate this using the chapter. (a) In which period did the style flourish in India? (b) Name the three traditions it blended. (c) Which of the three has the student left out? (d) Name two of its listed features and the traditions the chapter says inspired its patterns. (e) Give the chapter's example of a court building in this style and the year it was completed.
questions.a: (a) During the British Raj, from the mid-19th to the early 20th century. (b) Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements. (c) The Gothic, a European style; the student also treats Islamic elements as only Mughal. (d) Any two of domes, pointed arches, minarets and intricate decorative patterns; the patterns are inspired by Mughal and Rajput traditions. (e) The Madras High Court, completed in 1892. The student is therefore partly right about Mughal and Rajput inspiration but wrong to leave out the Gothic element and the Hindu elements.
s: Part (a): British Raj, mid-19th to early 20th century
Part (b): Islamic, Hindu and Gothic
Part (c): the Gothic element is missing
Part (d): two features and Mughal and Rajput inspiration
Part (e): Madras High Court, 1892

questions.q: A Shekhawati family lives in a very large old haveli. The upkeep is costly and the family is now small. What do these two facts match in the chapter's account of havelis?
questions.a: Havelis are hard to maintain and too large for today's families, so many are now hotels or museums
o: Havelis are hard to maintain and too large for today's families, so many are now hotels or museums
Havelis were built for single families, so the chapter says none has been opened to visitors at all
Havelis are cheap to keep, so the chapter says families still prefer to live in them today
Havelis were built as palaces by kings, so the state has taken them over and made them hotels

questions.q:
Match each building in Column A with the feature the chapter gives for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Madras High Court  2. St. Philomena's Cathedral, Mysuru  3. Kalloopara church, Travancore  4. St. Thomas Orthodox church, Mulanthuruthy
Column B: a. A sloped tiled roof typical of Kerala  b. A stambha borrowed from temple architecture  c. Islamic arches and screens beside Hindu temple-style carvings and pillars  d. The Gothic style, built in the colonial period

A project note on traditional houses says: (S1) 'The courtyard house began only in colonial times.' (S2) 'Courtyard houses were found only in cities.' (S3) 'The courtyard of a Chettinadu house was kept only for show.' Judge each statement with the chapter's evidence, rewrite S3 correctly, and (d) state in one line the design the chapter calls common in traditional houses.
questions.a: S1 wrong: some archaeologists remark that the design was already in use in some of the larger Harappan houses some 4,500 years ago. S2 wrong: the chapter says the design is common in traditional houses of the richer classes in both urban and rural contexts. S3 wrong: the central courtyard served as a place for rituals and community gatherings, and for sun-drying papads and chillies. Rewrite of S3: 'The courtyard of a Chettinadu house was used for rituals, community gatherings and sun-drying papads and chillies.' (d) A central courtyard with the rooms organised around it, over one or several storeys.
s: S1 judged wrong, with the Harappan evidence
